function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to run shell commands or push to a remote repository from here, but I can walk you through each step and give you the exact files you’ll need to add.  
Below is a “cheat‑sheet” you can copy‑paste into your terminal or editor.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with  
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create/update files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Assuming the repo contains a typical Node.js app (`app.js` or `index.js`) and a `package.json`, a minimal Dockerfile would look like this:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this version?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and includes the latest LTS.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * Exposing `3000` matches the default port used by many Node.js examples.

If the repo uses a different entry point (e.g., `server.js`), change the `CMD` line accordingly.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory called `k8s` (or `deployments`) and add two files:

#### `deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
```

#### `service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # change to NodePort or ClusterIP if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **How to apply**  
> ```bash
> kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
> kubectl apply -f k8s/service.yaml
> ```

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
      with:
        manifests: |
          k8s/deployment.yaml
          k8s/service.yaml
        images: |
          ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        namespace: default
        kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
```

> **Secrets you’ll need**  
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (not your password)  
> * `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` – base64‑encoded kubeconfig for the cluster you want to deploy to

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **What happens next?**  
> * GitHub Actions will automatically trigger on the push to `main`.  
> * It will build the Docker image, push it to Docker Hub, and deploy the new image to your Kubernetes cluster.

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile builds locally
docker build -t nodejs-welcome:local .

# Verify Kubernetes manifests apply locally (if you have a local cluster)
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/service.yaml
```

---

That’s it! Once the workflow finishes, your Node.js app should be running in Kubernetes, and the Docker image will be stored in Docker Hub. If you hit any snags, let me know and I’ll help troubleshoot.
